[[Image:Two-centerBipolarCoordinateSystem.JPG|right|frame|Two-center bipolar coordinates.]]

In [[mathematics]], '''two-center bipolar coordinates''' is a [[coordinate system]] based on two coordinates which give distances from two fixed centers <math>c_1</math> and <math>c_2</math>.<ref name=bip>{{mathworld|urlname=BipolarCoordinates|title=Bipolar coordinates}}</ref> This system is very useful in some scientific applications (e.g. calculating the [[electric field]] of a dipole on a plane).<ref>[http://www.physics.utah.edu/~rprice/AREA51DOCS/paperIIa.pdf R. Price, The Periodic Standing Wave Approximation: Adapted coordinates and spectral methods.]</ref><ref>[https://arxiv.org/abs/gr-qc/0502034v1 The periodic standing-wave approximation: nonlinear scalar fields, adapted coordinates, and the eigenspectral method.]</ref>

==Transformation to Cartesian coordinates==
When the centers are at <math>(+a, 0)</math> and <math>(-a, 0)</math>, the transformation to [[Cartesian coordinates]] <math>(x, y)</math> from two-center bipolar coordinates <math>(r_1, r_2)</math> is
:<math>x = \frac{r_2^2-r_1^2}{4a}</math>

:<math>y = \pm \frac{1}{4a}\sqrt{16a^2r_2^2-(r_2^2-r_1^2+4a^2)^2}</math><ref name=bip />

==Transformation to polar coordinates==
When ''x'' > 0, the transformation to [[polar coordinates]] from two-center bipolar coordinates is
:<math>r = \sqrt{\frac{r_1^2+r_2^2-2a^2}{2}}</math>

:<math>\theta = \arctan\left( \frac{\sqrt{r_1^4-8a^2r_1^2-2r_1^2r_2^2-(4a^2-r_2^2)^2}}{r_2^2-r_1^2} \right)</math> 
where <math>2 a</math> is the distance between the poles (coordinate system centers).

==Applications==
[[Polar plotter]]s use two-center bipolar coordinates to describe the drawing paths required to draw a target image.
